text: This case study is an illustrative, fictional scenario, not a real company or a real incident, built to make one specific failure mode concrete. Prairiewind Underwriters is a fictional regional insurance company that built a hub-and-spoke network almost identical in shape to the one from Lessons 29 and 30.

Prairiewind's architecture review board met twice and covered real, substantive ground: documented and tested RTO and RPO for claims processing and policy quoting, reviewed network segmentation between spokes, cost projections sized with headroom, and a compliance report showing every subscription passing its tagging rules. Every item was about the application tier. None of them was about the hub itself.

Eighteen months later, a regional outage took down the primary region for just under six hours. Both application databases failed over exactly on schedule, within their documented RTO. But the hub -- the firewall, the gateway, the DNS resolver -- existed only in the primary region, and had never been deployed to the secondary region. Every spoke's outbound route pointed at a firewall that no longer existed anywhere reachable.

Three individually reasonable factors combined into one blind spot: the review checklist was shaped around application workloads, so a shared network layer that no single team owned never appeared on it; ownership of the hub's DR plan was ambiguous between Platform and the application teams; and the architecture diagram's symmetric two-region drawing implied the secondary region was fully built out, when only the application boxes actually were.

One question, asked in either review session, would have surfaced the gap: if the primary region's hub goes down, what happens to every spoke that depends on it for egress and DNS, and is that dependency's own RTO and RPO documented anywhere? That single question forces shared services onto the same checklist as every application tier.

This is exactly what Lesson 30's ADR-003 does for Harlow Creek Logistics -- treating the hub as a DR-in-scope tier with its own explicit, tested RTO and RPO, deployed to both regions, instead of as background infrastructure nobody's checklist ever asked about. Lesson 32 closes the chapter by reviewing every decision across this whole course and naming what comes next.
